# Sleeping Through Countries: In Praise of the Night Train

There may be no better bargain left in the modern world than the one a night train offers. You arrive at a station in the evening, hand over a modest sum, climb into a narrow berth, switch off the reading lamp, and surrender consciousness. While you dream, the world does the work: bridges are crossed, borders slipped past, rivers forded in the dark. You wake beneath a different sky. Somewhere between closing your eyes and opening them again, you have been carried several hundred miles, and all you had to do was sleep. Air travel promises speed but delivers ordeal; the night train promises nothing except passage, and quietly delivers a kind of magic.

Consider what actually happens aboard one. Around ten o'clock, the corridor lights dim to a blue so faint it seems borrowed from the bottom of a swimming pool. The carriage settles into its long conversation with the rails — that two-note sway, *da-dum, da-dum*, sometimes smooth as a lullaby, sometimes broken by the sudden percussion of a junction, a shudder of couplings, the long moan of the horn at some unmanned crossing in the middle of nowhere. To the first-time traveler these sounds are an annoyance. To the initiated they are the point. The brain, presented with a rhythm both irregular and inevitable, does something curious: it stops negotiating with the noise and accepts it, folds it into sleep the way a shoreline folds waves into itself. Studies of rocking infants and swinging hammocks suggest the effect is physiological, not sentimental. The night train rocks you whether you consent or not, and somewhere around the second hour, you consent.

Then there is the compartment itself, that small wooden-and-formica cabin that is, for one night, the entire universe. The lower berth made up with sheets stiff from industrial laundering. The fold-down sink, gleaming chrome, with a cup chained beside it like a dog on a leash. The ladder up to the top bunk, where a stranger's shoes dangle at eye level. The window shade you pull down against the platforms, and the small brass latch that holds the door against the dark. Everything is miniature, everything is provisional, everything is exactly sufficient. There is a lesson in this economy that hotels costing five times as much have never learned: you do not need much room to sleep, only a little privacy and the sense that someone competent is driving.

The night train is old enough to have accumulated legends. George Pullman, an American carpenter turned industrialist, spent the 1860s perfecting the idea that a hotel did not have to stand still — his "palace cars" gave the transcontinental railways their velvet interiors, their porters, their folding upper berths that vanished into the ceiling by day. In Europe, the Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits took the conceit further: in October 1883, the first Orient Express pulled out of Paris bound for the East, and within a generation the sleeper had become the setting for a whole genre of human drama. Spies boarded them. Diplomats conducted the last negotiations of dying empires in their dining cars. Agatha Christie, stranded on the real thing by snowdrifts in Turkey in 1929, filed away the experience and produced, five years later, the most famous murder in railway history. The night train became shorthand for intrigue precisely because of what it is: a sealed world of strangers hurtling through darkness, everyone pretending to sleep, everyone technically alone and absolutely surrounded.

And that is the other great pleasure of the form — the temporary society of it. On a night train you are thrown into proximity with people you would never choose and will never see again, and this produces a peculiar etiquette, a diplomacy of the small hours. Where to look. When to speak. How to negotiate the shared use of a single electrical outlet. Conversations happen at midnight over instant coffee that would never survive daylight: a Hungarian engineer explaining why he distrusts both banks and governments; a student going home for a funeral, who tells you things she has told no one; an old man who rides this route twice a year and remembers when the dining car served pheasant. The night loosens tongues. There is something about being in transit, unmoored from your own address, that makes confession easy. By morning you will part at the platform with a handshake and no exchange of surnames, and this anonymity is not a failure of the encounter but its engine. The night train is one of the last places where strangers still talk to strangers, because it is one of the last places where strangers are locked into the same moving box with nothing to distract them but each other.

Meanwhile, outside the glass, the world goes by unseen. This is the strangest feature of night-train travel, and the hardest to explain to anyone who hasn't done it: you pass through entire countries without seeing them. Whole provinces, mountain ranges, the outskirts of cities whose names you'd recognize — all of it happens behind your eyelids, rendered only as sound. Occasionally you surface at three in the morning, some internal alarm tripped by the slowing of the wheels, and pull up the shade in time to catch a station sliding past: four lamps on a wet platform, a lone figure with a suitcase, a sign whose letters you cannot quite read before the darkness takes it back. Who was that person? Where were they going at this hour? You will never know, and neither will they know about you — two insomniac witnesses to each other's existence, exchanged for half a second across forty miles per hour. Then the train gathers itself, the rhythm resumes, and you sink back down into sleep like a stone into a well.

This is what the night train understands about time that airplanes refuse to admit: that transition is not dead time. The airport treats the journey as an inconvenience to be minimized — get them through security, get them into seats, get them off the plane, hurry, hurry. The night train treats the journey as a place in its own right, a country you visit between the countries on your itinerary. You are nowhere for eight hours, and the nowhere is furnished. Philosophers have a fondness for liminal states — thresholds, betwixt-and-between — but most of us rarely inhabit one deliberately. The night train is a threshold you can lie down in. It suspends you between addresses, between obligations, between versions of yourself: the person who boarded in the evening, tired and wired from the day's business, and the person who steps onto the platform at dawn, washed and remade, carrying nothing but a paper cup of coffee. Something small gets processed in those hours. Call it sleep if you like, but it feels more like being read a very long story you don't have to follow.

The borders deserve their own paragraph. For most of the twentieth century, crossing Europe by night meant the ritual of the passport check at two in the morning: the compartment door rattling open, the flashlight beam, the stamp, the door closing again, the train rolling on into a new jurisdiction while you lay there with your heart going. It was intrusive and slightly menacing and unforgettable — the state reaching into your sleep to verify you. Today, inside the Schengen zone, the crossings happen silently; you fly from Germany into France without waking, and the only evidence is a change in the overhead wires' hum. Some travelers mourn the stamps. But there is a deeper pleasure available now: the border as pure abstraction, a line drawn on a map that your sleeping body crosses without ceremony, proof that the divisions are ours and not the landscape's. The Danube doesn't show papers either.

It is worth pausing on how close we came to losing all of this. Through the 1990s and 2000s, the night train seemed finished. Budget airlines sold seats for less than the price of a taxi to the airport; high-speed day trains covered in four hours what sleepers covered in eight; national railways, losing money on every empty couchette, axed their overnight services one by one. By the mid-2010s, the obituaries were practically written. And then, oddly, the tide turned. Climate arithmetic began to trouble frequent flyers. Austria's federal railway, almost alone, doubled down — buying up rolling stock, branding its services, expanding route by route until "Nightjet" became a word known far beyond the Alps. Startups launched new sleeper lines between Brussels, Berlin, Amsterdam, Prague. France resurrected its classic overnight routes to Nice and the south. The arguments were practical — city center to city center, no hotel bill, a full working day on either end — but underneath them ran something less quantifiable: a suspicion that we had traded away something valuable in the name of speed, and a desire to buy it back.

Because the case for the night train was never really about efficiency. It is about what speed does to geography. At 900 kilometers per hour, the earth becomes an inconvenience — a gray-brown blur beneath cloud deck, erased between takeoff and landing. Distance stops being real and becomes merely annoying, a delay between the places that matter. The night train keeps the world's size honest. Even asleep, your body registers the distance: the curvature of the rails felt in the spine, the long climb into a mountain range announced by the laboring engines, the pause at some junction at dawn where freight trains wait in the fog. You arrive knowing, in your muscles, how big the country is. And you arrive slowly enough that the destination unfolds rather than assaults — first the outer ring of apartment blocks and allotment gardens, then the river, then the cranes of the port, then the station itself rising up with its iron-and-glass roof, and finally the platform, where the air smells of diesel and rain and whatever city this is.

Picture the whole arc once, end to end. Boarding at dusk, the platform loud with departures, finding your compartment and staking out the lower bunk. Dinner improvised on the fold-out table — bread, cheese, a bottle of wine bought at the station kiosk, the cork extracted with the confidence of someone who has done this before. Watching the suburbs thin out, the last allotments and warehouses giving way to genuine darkness, the window becoming a black mirror in which the compartment floats, ghostly, over the void. Turning in. The long negotiation with the pillow, the unfamiliar sounds resolving into rhythm. Waking once, briefly, to headlights sweeping the ceiling as the train passes through a town. Waking again to gray light and fog, pulling back the shade to discover — mountains? A river valley? The flat gold of a wheat plain running to the horizon under a sky the color of dishwater? Coffee in the dining car, the morning sun strobing through the windows in bars of light and shadow, the tables swaying gently on their pedestal legs, strangers reading newspapers in four languages. And then the announcement, the gathering of bags, the platform arriving to meet you, and the doors opening onto a day that begins already in motion.

There is a final thing the night train knows, and it may be the most important thing. Every night, millions of people entrust themselves, unconscious and utterly defenseless, to a machine operated by strangers, maintained by strangers, dispatched by strangers, traveling through territory owned by strangers — and it works. Almost always, it works. We speak constantly of declining trust, of institutions failing, of the fraying social contract, and there is truth in that litany. But then a person lies down in a metal box, closes their eyes, and lets the world carry them through the dark, and wakes up exactly where they intended to be. That is trust enacted at scale, nightly, without applause. The night train is a small monument to the quiet competence that holds civilization together: the signaler, the driver, the mechanic who torqued the bolts, the dispatcher watching the board at 4 a.m. None of them know you. All of them are keeping you.

So take the night train, sometime, while the taking is good. Book the couchette, pack the bread and cheese, learn the latch on the window. Let yourself be rocked through the dark at ground level, at human speed, through the actual world rather than above it. Wake to a foreign platform and walk out into a city that owes you nothing yet. Between every departure and every arrival there stretches a country that appears on no map — the country of the in-between, of the swaying dark, of strangers' voices and unreadable station signs. The night train is the only vehicle that lets you live there instead of merely passing through. Sleep well. The world is driving.
